items: `@?` = does this path return at least one item
`@@` = evaluate a path that IS a predicate, return its boolean
Mixing the two up is the classic beginner error
Functions mirror them: `jsonb_path_exists`, `jsonb_path_match`
Plus `jsonb_path_query`, `_query_first`, `_query_array`

blocks.title: Indexing Caveat
blocks.text: GIN accelerates `@?`/`@@` only for shapes it can reduce to containment: plain key accessors with `==`. Ranges, regex, and `.**` fall back to a full scan of the candidate set.

items: GIN is an inverted index: extracted key to the rows containing it
Exactly the structure for 'which documents contain this bit'

slides.page_title: GIN Recheck & Lax vs Strict Paths

items: GIN stores no reconstructable value — every match rechecks the heap tuple
Expect `Bitmap Index Scan` + `Bitmap Heap Scan` with `Recheck Cond`
Never an index-only scan
`jsonb_path_ops` hash collisions give false positives; recheck filters them

blocks.note: recheck is normal, not a bug

blocks.title: @? or @@?
blocks.text: `@?` takes a **locator** and asks if it finds anything; `@@` takes a **predicate** and returns its boolean. Filters use `?()` with `@` as the current item.

items: Indexing one subtree gives a fraction of the size
`data->'tags' @> ...` will not use an index built on `data`
Partial GIN keeps a hot subset tiny
GIN inserts are expensive
`fastupdate = on` (default) buffers them in a pending list
VACUUM or `gin_pending_list_limit` flushes it
A query may scan the pending list — latency spikes

items: Drop the GIN index, `COPY`, rebuild
Far cheaper than row-by-row maintenance
Raise `maintenance_work_mem` for the rebuild
`btree_gin`: `gin (tenant_id, data jsonb_path_ops)`
GIN cannot help range, sort, or unique constraints
For those, index the extracted scalar with btree
The cast goes inside the index AND inside the query
The cast must be IMMUTABLE — `::timestamptz` from text is not
Store UTC and cast to `timestamp`, or use a stable helper
Uniqueness inside a document: one of the few real constraints jsonb carries

slides.page_title: TOAST, Planner Stats & When jsonb Fits

items: A row wider than ~2 KB pushes jsonb out of line and compresses it
Reading one key detoasts and decompresses the WHOLE document
There is no partial read of a jsonb field
`SELECT data->>'id'` on a 200 KB document does 200 KB of work per row

blocks.title: SET STORAGE EXTERNAL
blocks.text: `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN data SET STORAGE EXTERNAL` skips compression: bigger on disk, cheaper CPU per read. Measure before adopting. Narrow, hot fields belong in columns, not deep in a fat document.

items: Postgres collects no per-key statistics for jsonb
`@>` selectivity is a fixed guess, roughly 0.1%, however common the value
Wrong estimates feed wrong join orders and nested loops over millions
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and compare estimated vs actual rows

blocks.title: Why It Actually Got Faster
blocks.text: A generated column gets real statistics — histograms, MCVs, `n_distinct`. That, not the index, is often the real reason. Prefer btree on a generated column whenever the key is always present.

blocks.title: Storage Overhead
items: Every row repeats every key name
A million rows pay for `"description"` a million times
A column stores the name once, in the catalog

blocks.title: Why Large Hurts
blocks.text: Every jsonb update rewrites the whole row and re-TOASTs the whole value. Frequent small writes into a fat document are the classic mistake.

items: Attributes are sparse, unbounded, or caller-defined
Webhook payloads, per-tenant custom fields, flags, event properties
The access pattern is whole-document read/write
The shape versions faster than you can ship migrations

slides.page_title: When a Column Wins & The Hybrid Schema

items: The field is filtered, joined, sorted, or aggregated on
You get statistics, btree indexes, and plans that do not guess
You need integrity: NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, especially FOREIGN KEY
A jsonb field can never reference another table
The field updates often and the document is large
jsonb as an EAV replacement is a genuine win
One indexed column beats an attribute table with a self-join per attribute
Stable core as columns, variable tail as jsonb
Promote hot jsonb keys to generated columns over time
Postgres allows 1600 columns; a document counts as one

items: A 40 KB document holding a hit counter
`@> '{"qty":5}'` against a stored `"qty": "5"`
Read-modify-write without `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`
The scalar-in-array exception does not reach nested levels
Duplicate keys never survive a jsonb round trip
Concatenated JSON is a JSON-injection hole, not a style choice
Only the first form of each pair can use a GIN index
Filter with ==`@>`== first, unnest the survivors after
`jsonb_path_ops` unless you need `?` existence
Promote a key the moment it becomes **load-bearing**

blocks.title: One Line
blocks.text: jsonb is a parsed, ordered, indexable structure; `@>` plus GIN is the fast path; jsonpath is the expressive path; expression and generated columns supply the constraints and statistics jsonb lacks — and the moment a key becomes load-bearing, promote it to a column.

caption.text: Part 2 of POSTGRES JSONB. Most Postgres jsonb bugs are not bugs — they are two operators that look identical and behave nothing alike. `data->>'k' = 'v'` cannot touch a GIN index; `data @> '{"k":"v"}'` can. Ten pages on storage, containment, jsonpath, GIN opclasses, TOAST, and the exact moment a key stops belonging in the document.
